outcome: Nothing has settled the problem since 26 January 2024. The degree-3 instance is still partly open: a 2022 journal-accepted periodicity result covers only totally real cubics, and the complex-signature cubic case, which Karpenkov left open, has two unrefereed single-author preprints from August 2026 giving conditional and sample-based evidence and stating that the general problem remains open. Degrees 4 and above show no movement; degrees 1 and 2 are classical.
problem_asks: For every natural number n: whether there is an assignment, to each real number x, of a sequence of natural numbers such that the sequence for x is eventually periodic if and only if x is algebraic of degree exactly n. Unpacked: (a) for each n separately, one assignment defined for every real x (the statement says 'to each real number'; it does not ask for a single uniform algorithm across n); (b) the forward direction: every algebraic x of degree n has an eventually periodic sequence; (c) the converse: every x whose sequence is eventually periodic is algebraic of degree exactly n (not merely of degree at most n); (d) the sequence is a function of the single real x. Instances: n=1 (rationals; decimal expansions); n=2 (quadratic irrationals; continued fractions); n=3 (cubic irrationals, the instance the Wikipedia lead names, with its totally real and complex-signature sub-cases); n>=4 (algebraic numbers of degree at least 4, which the Wikipedia article calls 'algebraic numbers of any fixed degree d').

events.what_happened: Classical fact: decimal (base-10) expansions of rationals are eventually periodic and those of irrationals are not. The Wikipedia article's Motivation section cites this as the degree-1 case. I found no originating publication and no date, so the event is recorded undated. It settles the n=1 instance, with the caveat that the statement does not say how to encode the sign of negative reals in natural-number digits.
events.delivers: Settles n=1: for nonnegative x, the digit sequence is eventually periodic exactly when x is rational (degree 1). Negative x need a sign convention that the statement leaves implicit.
events.remains: Nothing for n=1 beyond the sign convention.
events.directly_checkable: Long division shows that the digits of a rational are eventually periodic; the converse is the standard argument that a periodic digit tail is a rational.
events.direction: Agrees with the statement: the n=1 instance holds.

events.what_happened: The quadratic case (n=2): the continued-fraction expansion of x is eventually periodic if and only if x is a quadratic irrational. Per the Wikipedia article, Euler's Introductio (1748) gives the expansions and Lagrange proved the periodicity result in 1770. I did not open either original; the attribution is from the Wikipedia article.
events.delivers: Settles n=2 completely, with continued-fraction digits (natural numbers): eventual periodicity holds exactly for quadratic irrationals. Rationals have finite expansions, which are not infinite periodic sequences; the statement leaves that convention implicit.
events.remains: Nothing for n=2.

checked_by.who: Lagrange (periodicity theorem) and Euler (expansions), as credited by the Wikipedia article
checked_by.what_they_did: Proved the periodicity result (Lagrange, 1770) and gave the continued-fraction expansions (Euler, 1748), per Wikipedia

events.directly_checkable: Standard: the continued fraction of a quadratic surd such as sqrt(2) = [1; 2, 2, 2, ...] is checkable by hand.
events.direction: Agrees with the statement: the n=2 instance holds.

events.what_happened: Thomas Garrity, 'On periodic sequences for algebraic numbers' (arXiv math/9906016, v1 2 June 1999, v3 13 August 1999). Gives a new expansion for each integer n >= 2 with n=2 matching the continued-fraction algorithm; for n=3 it is an iteration on the triangle, and for general n an iteration on an n-simplex. The abstract (as summarised by the fetch tool) shows that cubic irrationals that are roots of x^3 + k x^2 + x - 1 have purely periodic expansions of period length one. No journal reference is listed on the arXiv page. The arXiv page does not mention Hermite's problem.
events.revisions: v1 2 Jun 1999; v2 18 Jun 1999; v3 13 Aug 1999 (current).
events.delivers: For n=3 only: a family of cubic polynomials (x^3 + k x^2 + x - 1, with k not further restricted in the sources I read) whose roots have purely periodic expansions. For general n, a construction giving periodic expansions for certain algebraic numbers. No characterisation of eventual periodicity; no converse.
events.remains: Every cubic irrational outside the special family; the converse direction for all n; every n>=4 instance as a characterisation.
events.directly_checkable: Roots of the stated polynomials and their expansions under Garrity's map are checkable by hand for small k, but I did not do so.
events.direction: Partial and in the direction of the statement (periodic expansions for a special cubic family). It is a construction, not a characterisation.
events.object: A construction, not a single object: for n=3 the expansion map on the triangle, with the stated cubic polynomials having purely periodic expansions of period length one. Explicit, not an existence proof.

events.what_happened: Olga Beaver and Thomas Garrity, 'A Two-Dimensional Minkowski ?(x) Function' (arXiv math/0210480, v1 31 Oct 2002, v2 8 Dec 2002). Defines a continuous bijection of a triangle onto itself. Per the abstract (summarised), a natural class of pairs of cubic irrationals in one cubic field maps to pairs of rationals. The arXiv page does not mention Hermite's problem or periodicity. The 2004 Journal of Number Theory publication comes from a search snippet and I did not open it.
events.revisions: v1 31 Oct 2002; v2 8 Dec 2002 (current). Journal of Number Theory 107 (2004) per search snippet, not verified.
events.delivers: Not a periodicity result. It maps pairs of cubic irrationals to pairs of rationals, which is a different object from an expansion assigned to each real number. Discounted as an analogue.
events.remains: All of the problem, as the statement is about periodic sequences rather than a question-mark function.
events.direction: Does not bear on the periodicity question; the object is a function on pairs, not a sequence assignment.

events.what_happened: Krishna Dasaratha, Laure Flapan, Thomas Garrity, Chansoo Lee, Cornelia Mihaila, Nicholas Neumann-Chun, Sarah Peluse and Matthew Stoffregen, 'Cubic Irrationals and Periodicity via a Family of Multi-dimensional Continued Fraction Algorithms' (arXiv 1208.4244, v1 21 Aug 2012, v5 26 Apr 2014). Per the abstract: builds a countable family of multidimensional continued-fraction algorithms from five maps; identifies a broad class of cubic irrationals a for which (a, a^2) or (a, a - a^2) is purely periodic under some map in the family; for each cubic field, some pair (u, u') built from a unit has a periodic expansion under one of the maps. The abstract ends by recasting the link as a question about nonnegative integer matrices with an eventually periodic row. The arXiv page lists 'to appear in Monatshefte fur Mathematik'; a search snippet gives Monatsh. Math. 174 (4), 549-566 (2014), not verified in the publisher record.
events.revisions: v1 21 Aug 2012; v2 20 Jan 2013; v3 9 Jan 2014; v4 12 Jan 2014; v5 26 Apr 2014 (current). Journal: Monatshefte fur Mathematik, 2014 (per search snippet).
events.delivers: Periodic expansions (not a characterisation) for a broad class of cubic irrationals under some map in a countable family; for each cubic field, periodic expansion of some unit-built pair. Inputs are pairs derived from the cubic irrational or from a unit, not a single real number assigned a sequence. Restricted to the listed cubic classes.
events.remains: A single assignment for every cubic irrational; the converse (periodic implies cubic) for the family; all n other than 3 as characterisations.

checked_by.who: Monatshefte fur Mathematik (Springer), journal of record
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the paper for publication, per the arXiv 'to appear' note and a search snippet (2014). Referee reports not visible.

events.directly_checkable: The expansions for specific cubic units are checkable by hand, but I did not check any.
events.doubts: The abstract I opened does not mention Hermite's problem. Search summaries say the paper argues that one algorithm probably cannot solve the problem and that a family is needed, but I did not read the full text to confirm this.
events.direction: Partial, toward the statement: periodicity for a broad class of cubic irrationals under a family of algorithms, not one assignment.
events.object: Periodic expansions for specific classes: pairs (a, a^2) or (a, a - a^2) with a in a listed cubic class, and pairs (u, u') built from a unit in each cubic field, under one of five explicit maps. Explicit construction, not an existence proof.

events.what_happened: Nadir Murru, 'On the Hermite problem for cubic irrationalities' (arXiv 1305.3285, v1 14 May 2013, v2 10 Nov 2013, v3 16 Jan 2014). The arXiv abstract (as summarised by the fetch tool) gives a periodic representation, by periodic rational or integer sequences, for any cubic irrationality. It is a periodic multidimensional continued fraction with pre-period 2 and period 3, from a modified Jacobi algorithm, proved to converge to the given cubic irrational. The abstract also says the modified algorithm is periodic if and only if the inputs are cubic irrationals, and that the representation gives simultaneous rational approximations. The fetch summary quotes the abstract as saying the problem 'has been solved'; I could not read that sentence verbatim. A companion arXiv 1304.2906 (Abrate, Barbero, Cerruti, Murru; Fibonacci Quarterly 50(3), 2012) was not opened. The later version (Politecnico di Torino repository, hermite.pdf) says the Hermite problem 'cannot be claimed completely solved', because the representation does not come from an algorithm defined over all real numbers; that PDF returned 403 and I did not open it. Wikipedia repeats the caveat and says the representation is derived from the minimal polynomial.
events.revisions: v1 14 May 2013; v2 10 Nov 2013; v3 16 Jan 2014 (current, per arXiv). Published in International Journal of Number Theory 11 (2015) per the Wikipedia citation, not verified. The later Politecnico version carries the caveat that the problem cannot be claimed completely solved.
events.delivers: For n=3, forward direction: each cubic irrational has an eventually periodic representation by a construction that uses the cubic's minimal polynomial. The construction is not an algorithm defined on all real numbers, so it does not give a single assignment to each real x (the author's own later caveat, and Wikipedia). The arXiv abstract's periodic-if-and-only-if claim is for the modified Jacobi algorithm on cubic inputs.
events.remains: A single assignment to every real number (not dependent on the minimal polynomial); the converse for single real inputs; every n other than 3.
events.directly_checkable: The representation for a specific cubic (for example 2^(1/3)) could be checked by computing its periodic tail; I did not do so.
events.doubts: The arXiv abstract's 'has been solved' wording (as summarised) conflicts with the later version and with Wikipedia, which say the problem cannot be claimed completely solved. I found no referee report or expert verification of the claim. The published version and its caveat were not verified, since the Politecnico PDF returned 403.
events.direction: Toward the statement for n=3 (cubic implies eventually periodic) through a minimal-polynomial-dependent construction. Whether it satisfies the statement's form, one assignment to each real, is disputed by the author's later version and by Wikipedia.
events.object: A periodic multidimensional continued fraction with pre-period 2 and period 3, built from a modified Jacobi algorithm, converging to a given cubic irrational. Explicit given the cubic's minimal polynomial, as Wikipedia states; not an existence proof.

events.what_happened: Nadir Murru, 'Linear recurrence sequences and periodicity of multidimensional continued fractions' (arXiv 1712.08810, 23 Dec 2017; The Ramanujan Journal 44 (2017) 115-124 per the arXiv page). Characterises when the Jacobi-Perron algorithm is periodic: partial quotients are periodic exactly when the numerators and denominators of the convergents are linear recurrence sequences. The abstract (summarised) says no algorithm then produced a periodic multidimensional continued fraction from a given algebraic irrationality. The page does not mention Hermite's problem or cubic irrationals.
events.delivers: A characterisation of periodicity for the Jacobi-Perron algorithm in terms of linear recurrence sequences. It is about that algorithm's periodicity and not about an assignment for each degree. As of 2017 it records that no algorithm produced periodic expansions from a given algebraic irrational.
events.remains: The statement's assignment for every n; the Jacobi-Perron periodicity is not shown to characterise any degree.

checked_by.who: The Ramanujan Journal (Springer), journal of record
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper, Vol. 44 No. 1, pp. 115-124 (2017), per the arXiv page

events.direction: Neighbouring: about periodicity of a known algorithm, not a new assignment. Its statement that no algorithm yet gives periodic expansions from a given algebraic irrational is itself a status note for 2017.

events.what_happened: Nadir Murru and Lea Terracini, 'On the finiteness and periodicity of the p-adic Jacobi-Perron algorithm' (arXiv 1901.04922, 15 Jan 2019). Studies finiteness and periodicity of the p-adic analogue of the Jacobi-Perron algorithm; periodic expansions of dimension m converge to algebraic irrationals of degree at most m+1, with more detail for m=2. The page does not mention Hermite's problem.
events.delivers: Results about the p-adic analogue. Discounted as a different question: it is over the p-adic numbers, not the reals, and gives a degree bound for periodic expansions rather than an assignment.
events.remains: All of the real-number problem.
events.direction: Analogue only; it does not bear on the real-number statement.

events.what_happened: George Jacobs, 'Algorithm to Detect Periodicity by Interleaving Sequences' (arXiv 1905.08065, v1 16 May 2019 UTC). Gives an algorithm that takes a sequence of sequences and outputs one sequence, so that periodicity of the output tail matches periodicity of an input tail. It supplements Dasaratha et al.: at least one of a countable family of sequences attached to a real input is eventually periodic if and only if the input is a cubic irrational. The author states that this does not give a satisfying resolution to Hermite's problem.
events.revisions: v1 16 May 2019 only (arXiv UTC timestamp; a search listing gives 15 May 2019 in US time).
events.delivers: An iff for cubic irrationals, but with a countable family of sequences per real input, of which one is eventually periodic exactly for cubic inputs. It does not assign a single sequence to each real. The author says it does not resolve the problem.
events.remains: The single-sequence version of the statement; every n other than 3 as a characterisation.
events.doubts: The author's own statement that the approach 'fails to give a satisfying resolution to Hermite's problem'. The family-of-sequences form departs from a single assignment.
events.direction: Partial: an iff for cubic inputs, but in a family form the author says does not resolve the question.
events.object: A construction: a countable family of sequences per real input, of which one is eventually periodic if and only if the input is a cubic irrational, built by interleaving the sequences of a Dasaratha et al. expansion. Explicit, not an existence proof.

events.what_happened: Oleg Karpenkov, 'On a periodic Jacobi-Perron type algorithm' (arXiv 2101.12627, v1 29 Jan 2021, v2 16 Feb 2021). Introduces a modification of the Jacobi-Perron algorithm in dimension three and proves its periodicity for totally real conjugate cubic vectors. The fetch summary quotes the abstract as presenting this as an answer, in the totally real case, to Hermite's question on algebraic periodicity. Whether this preprint is the same argument as the Monatshefte article in event karpenkov-2024-monatshefte is not established.
events.revisions: v1 29 Jan 2021 (58 KB); v2 16 Feb 2021 (59 KB, current). Possibly superseded by the Monatshefte article (unverified).
events.delivers: Periodicity for the modified Jacobi-Perron algorithm on totally real conjugate cubic vectors. The input is a vector of conjugates, which presupposes the minimal polynomial (inferred from 'totally-real conjugate cubic vectors'; not spelled out in the abstract I read). It establishes forward periodicity for totally real cubic irrationals; the converse is not stated in the abstract I read.
events.remains: The complex-conjugate-root cubic case; the converse (periodic implies cubic); a single real input rather than a conjugate vector; every n other than 3.
events.direction: Toward the statement for n=3, restricted to totally real cubic conjugate vectors.
events.object: A modified Jacobi-Perron map on conjugate cubic vectors, shown periodic for totally real cubic irrationals. Periodicity is proved, not an explicit expansion of a named number.

events.what_happened: Oleg Karpenkov, 'On Hermite's problem, Jacobi-Perron type algorithms, and Dirichlet groups' (arXiv 2101.12707, v1 29 Jan 2021; published Acta Arithmetica 203 (2022), 27-48, DOI 10.4064/aa210614-5-1). Per the arXiv abstract (summarised by the fetch tool): introduces a heuristic algebraic periodicity-detecting algorithm (HAPD in later sources), whose output is periodic on many cubic irrationals but whose periodicity is not proven; and the sin^2-algorithm, periodic for all totally real cubic irrationals. The abstract states that the case of cubic algebraic numbers with complex conjugate roots remains open. The abstract also says the paper ends with an application to independent elements in maximal commuting groups of matrices.
events.revisions: v1 29 Jan 2021 only on the arXiv page. Acta Arithmetica 203 (2022) per the journal listing; the journal date does not move the event.
events.delivers: Periodicity of the sin^2-algorithm for totally real cubic irrationals (restricted to the totally real class). The heuristic algorithm is explicitly unproven for cubic irrationals. The complex case is listed as open.
events.remains: Complex-conjugate-root cubics; the heuristic algorithm's periodicity; the converse; a single real input; every n other than 3.

checked_by.who: Acta Arithmetica (Institute of Mathematics, Polish Academy of Sciences), journal of record
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted and published the paper, vol. 203 (2022), pp. 27-48, per the IMPAN listing. Referee reports not visible.

events.directly_checkable: The heuristic algorithm can be run on a given cubic irrational by hand for small examples; I did not do so.
events.doubts: The heuristic algorithm's periodicity is unproven, as the authors say. I read only the abstract, not the full text.
events.direction: Toward the statement for n=3, totally real case only. The complex case is explicitly open in the paper.
events.object: The sin^2-algorithm, a Jacobi-Perron-type map on cubic vectors, proved periodic for every totally real cubic irrational; and a heuristic algorithm observed periodic on many examples, unproven. Explicit maps, periodicity proved for the first and not for the second.

events.what_happened: Y. Sifontes and D. Tejada, 'Aproximacion Dinamica al Problema de Hermite' (arXiv 2305.19808, 31 May 2023, in Spanish). Starts from the quadratic case and asks whether it extends to cubic irrationals, using a piecewise continuous function f_Gamma tied to the modular group (Edward and Series, 1978). Per the arXiv abstract (summarised by the fetch tool), the authors claim f_Gamma gives infinite periodic continued-fraction representations for quadratic irrationals and non-periodic infinite representations for non-quadratic irrationals. The PDF returned an unreadable compressed stream, so the abstract wording is from the abstract page's summary and is not verbatim.
events.delivers: If the summary is right: for the n=2 instance, a single map with periodicity exactly for quadratic irrationals. For n=3 the claim is that all cubic irrationals are non-periodic under this map, which is the opposite of what the n=3 instance needs (cubic implies periodic). So it would not settle the statement for n=3 even if correct.
events.remains: The n=3 instance (periodicity of cubic irrationals) would be contradicted by the claim if it were read as a claim about the statement's sequences; every n other than 2.
events.doubts: Read from the abstract summary only; the paper is in Spanish and its text was not readable here. No review, citation or response found in my searches.
events.direction: As summarised, the non-quadratic non-periodicity claim cuts against the n=3 instance of the statement; the quadratic claim is the classical n=2 case.
events.object: A map f_Gamma, tied to the modular group, giving periodic expansions for quadratic irrationals and claimed non-periodic expansions for others. Explicit, but I could not read its definition or proof.

Main subject is m-dimer covers on snake graphs. The abstract mentions Hermite's problem for cubic irrationals once, calling the generalised continued fractions 'a possibly novel approach towards Hermite's problem for cubic irrationals'. No result on the problem is claimed.
events.delivers: Nothing on the problem: the Hermite remark is a proposed application, not a result. Discounted.
events.remains: All of the problem.
events.direction: Does not bear on the problem beyond a stated potential application.

Math. 42 (2024) 125571 per the arXiv page). Describes the repetend matrices of eventually periodic expansions in the Algebraic Jacobi-Perron Algorithm, gives criteria for purely periodic expansions and shows certain vectors have eventually periodic expansions. The page does not mention Hermite's problem or cubic irrationals.

The abstract does not say whether it bears on periodicity or on the Hermite question.

events.what_happened: Oleg Karpenkov, article in Monatshefte fur Mathematik, DOI 10.1007/s00605-024-02006-5 (Springer). I could not open the article: the Springer page and PDF redirected to an identity-provider page. From a search snippet of its Introduction, the paper introduces the sin^2-algorithm, proves its periodicity for totally real cubic vectors, and presents this as a solution, in the totally real case, of a version called the 'Three Hermite Problem'. The snippet also says the author describes it as the first algorithm proven periodic if and only if applied to cubic vectors (the iff is for cubic vectors in the totally real case). Tagnon's preprint quotes Problem 4 from this paper's Section 9: find a generalised Euclidean algorithm that is periodic for real cubic vectors in the non-totally-real case.
events.revisions: The DOI year (2024) is the only date evidence I have. The mathematics may be the same as arXiv 2101.12627 (29 Jan 2021); if so, the first public written argument predates the frozen revision. Not resolved.

events.remains: The complex-signature (non-totally-real) cubic case (Problem 4); a single real input rather than a vector of conjugates; every n other than 3.

The abstract page does not mention Hermite's problem or its status. A search snippet said the paper calls Hermite's problem for degree above two open; the PDF returned unreadable compressed content, so that claim is unverified and may be wrong.

events.what_happened: Brandon Barclay, 'Solving Hermite's Problem: Three Novel Approaches for Complete Characterization of Cubic Irrationals' (2025). Known only from a third-party interactive-visualisation page (science.ecosyste.ms/projects/138626, CC BY 4.0), whose BibTeX lists it as an 'arXiv preprint' with a placeholder URL (arxiv.org/abs/xxxx.xxxxx). The page could not be opened (HTTP 403). The snippet describes three methods: a projective-space periodicity detector (HAPD-based), a companion-matrix and trace-sequence approach to continued-fraction expansions, and a third described as a modified sin^2 algorithm for complex conjugate roots. It claims 'complete characterization' of cubic irrationals. I found no arXiv listing: a guessed arXiv author-listing URL returned 404, which is not conclusive, and title searches found nothing.
events.delivers: As claimed on the page: a complete characterisation for cubic irrationals (both real and complex-signature). Not verifiable: no arXiv identifier, no text read.
events.remains: If the claim were verified, nothing for n=3; every n other than 3 would remain open.
events.doubts: No arXiv identifier, and the BibTeX URL is a placeholder. The claim of complete characterisation conflicts with the literature recorded here: the complex-conjugate case is open per Karpenkov's abstract, and Murru's later version says the problem cannot be claimed completely solved. Promotional wording in the snippet. I could not confirm that a paper of this title exists.
events.direction: If the claim is what the page says, it would cut toward the statement for n=3 in full, but I could not verify it exists or what it proves.

events.what_happened: Ludovic Tagnon (sole author; ORCID 0009-0000-6456-3476 per Zenodo; 'Nancy, France' per the fetched PDF text), 'A deterministic sin2-type algorithm for complex cubic irrationalities with exact periodicity certificates'. Zenodo manuscript DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21222498 (published 6 Jul 2026, v1, the only version I found); same title and abstract on arXiv 2608.23281 (submitted 24 Aug 2026, v1, math.NT, labelled 'Part I of a series'). The paper targets the complex-signature (1,1) case that Karpenkov left open (Problem 4). Its abstract reports: on 205 sample complex cubic polynomials every run closed projectively with an exact unit certificate; an exhaustive run over [-3,3]^3 closed 194 of 194; across 457 deformed bases the terminal cycle appears invariant; certified finite transition graphs for four fields; the plastic case machine-checked in Lean 4. It states 'The general periodicity problem remains open.' Section 1 says: 'It does not solve the complex case of Hermite's problem: no general periodicity theorem is proved here.' Conjecture 4.1 (every admissible trajectory eventually periodic) and Conjecture 4.2 (common terminal cycle) are stated and marked open. Theorem B (Section 6.2): the explicit 2285-state plastic-field closure has a single cycle of length 1 that every state reaches. Lemma 2.4: a projective return with positive real unit gives eventual periodicity. Section 7.2 reports that literal HAPD (Karpenkov's conjectural heuristic) halts on 155 of 205 polynomials, with 80 empty-candidate halts and 75 integer-characteristic ties; the authors say the published HAPD definition specifies no tie-break and that they read the halts as a feature of the heuristic, not a defect.
events.revisions: Zenodo manuscript v1, 6 Jul 2026. arXiv 2608.23281 v1, 24 Aug 2026 (PDF 893.4 KB; Zenodo PDF 892.7 kB), not compared text by text. Zenodo reproducibility archive (10.5281/zenodo.21182759; record reached via zenodo.org; versions listed up to v10, last modified 8 Oct 2026, with note 'verifier strengthened; no computed datum modified').
events.delivers: Restricted to sampled and certified cases: exact unit certificates for periodicity on 205 sample complex cubic polynomials and on 194 polynomials in the box [-3,3]^3; finite transition graphs for four fields; plastic-field closure (one cycle). It proves structural lemmas (Lemma 2.4 propagation; score negative on signature (1,1) data). It proves no general periodicity theorem, by its own statement. The totally real case is cited as solved by Karpenkov.
events.remains: Periodicity for all complex cubic irrationals (Conjecture 4.1); the common terminal cycle (Conjecture 4.2); the converse direction; single real inputs; every n other than 3; the totally real case is not treated here.

machine_checked.system: Lean 4 (kernel-only, under the standard axioms; a sealed layer under lean/ per the Zenodo description)

events.directly_checkable: Per the Zenodo description, verify_all.py (standard library, about ten minutes) rechecks the headline numbers, re-certifies 2,277 exact unit norms and 654 equations in exact cubic-field arithmetic, and recomputes the 2,285-state plastic score map; make_all.py regenerates the Section 3 tables from 205 polynomials. I did not download or run the archive (117.3 MB).
events.doubts: (1) Zenodo dataset description: 'This work was assisted by AI', 'no independent mathematician has reviewed the work yet', and 'mechanical verification does not confirm the statements express the intended mathematics'. (2) The Lean check covers the plastic transition graph and a 'machine-checked core' (Part I abstract and Section 8.2), not the periodicity theorem; the paper says the exact scope is in Section 8, which I read only in part. I did not confirm the absence of sorry in the Lean sources. (3) Periodicity is shown on samples and by certificates for specific fields, not for all cubic fields; the paper says so. (4) The Zenodo archive was revised after posting (v10, 8 Oct 2026: 'verifier strengthened; no computed datum modified'). (5) Two Zenodo DOIs appear for the dataset (21182759 and 22081378); I used 21182759.
events.direction: Toward the statement for complex cubic fields (cubic implies eventually periodic), by certified evidence on samples and fields; no general theorem is claimed. The paper's own Problem 4 quotation asks for a generalised Euclidean algorithm periodic for real cubic vectors in the non-totally-real case; this paper does not fully meet that. The authors describe their result as not solving the complex case.
events.object: The deterministic sin2-type algorithm on complex-signature cubic states, with a declared tie-break order and a selection rule minimising a score (negative on signature (1,1) data). Its periodicity is exhibited by exact unit certificates on 205 sample polynomials, on the 194 polynomials of [-3,3]^3, and by a finite transition graph for four fields, the plastic field included (closure to one cycle, Lean-checked). No counterexample to periodicity is exhibited.

events.what_happened: Ludovic Tagnon, 'A dual reformulation of the complex sin^2-algorithm: exact identities, descent, and finiteness' (arXiv 2608.24750, submitted 25 Aug 2026, v1 only on the abstract page; math.NT; 28 pages; labelled Part II; its Comments field says the contraction hypothesis (C_kappa) is discharged in Paper III, which I could not find). Gives the structure theory of the Part I algorithm: the selection rule is the minimisation of a conformal module (the hyperbolic cosine of a distance); a one-step growth bound of phi^2; finiteness of states of bounded module and height at fixed coordinate discriminant; a height bound. Per-field periodicity (Theorem 4.6) is proved under (C_kappa) plus an orbit condition (B); Theorem 4.14 removes (B) given (C_kappa). (C_kappa) is only partly reduced to a compact inequality (R), which the paper calls a 'compact inequality currently targeted' and which is not proved. Section 8 says 'Three design choices make the entire chain machine-checkable', and the abstract says a machine-checked core is sealed in Lean 4 (kernel-only, standard axioms). Section 9 (fetched text): 'The structural identities of Sections 2-5 and the height-descent theorem are proved.' and 'This manuscript proves neither statement.' The statements the second sentence refers to are not clear from my extraction.
events.revisions: arXiv 2608.24750 v1, 25 Aug 2026, the only version on the abstract page. One search summary said v2 was an editorial revision after external review; the abstract page lists only v1, so this is unresolved.
events.delivers: Conditional: per-field eventual periodicity for complex-signature cubic fields, conditional on (C_kappa) (and (B) in the original form, removed under (C_kappa)). (C_kappa) is itself reduced only partly, to (R), which is not proved. The structural identities, one-step growth bound, finiteness and height descent are proved, per the paper. No unconditional periodicity theorem.
events.remains: Unconditional periodicity for any complex cubic field; (C_kappa) and (R); the converse; the totally real case beyond Karpenkov; single real inputs; every n other than 3.

machine_checked.system: Lean 4 (kernel-only, standard axioms; 'a machine-checked core of the paper')

events.doubts: (1) Conditional: (C_kappa) is not proved, and (R) is stated as a target and not proved (paper's own words). (2) Per search summaries, the one hypothesis is partly reduced to a finite minimax checked by sampled sweeps and a floating-point pass, not a full proof, and several subcases are described as open. (3) No independent review found. (4) The Comments field refers to a Paper III that I could not find.
events.direction: Conditional toward the statement for complex cubic fields. If (C_kappa) holds, per-field periodicity follows; the paper does not establish (C_kappa).

disputes.summary: Murru's arXiv abstract (2013, as summarised) says the problem of writing cubic irrationals as periodic sequences has been solved, while Murru's later version, Wikipedia and the Karpenkov/Tagnon line of work describe the problem as open, because the periodic representation depends on the minimal polynomial and is not an algorithm defined on all reals. Not resolved here.

Barclay's 2025 page claims a 'complete characterization' of cubic irrationals; Karpenkov's abstract says the complex-conjugate-root case remains open, and Tagnon's 2026 Part I says it does not solve that case. No arXiv identifier for the Barclay claim was found.
Accossato, Murru and Romeo (2025) might call the degree-above-two problem open: one search summary says so, but the abstract page does not mention Hermite's problem and the PDF was unreadable.

summary: The problem has been settled only in its low-degree instances, and those long ago: rationals by decimal expansions (n=1) and quadratic irrationals by continued fractions (n=2, Lagrange 1770). For n=3 the record shows a partial, uneven history. Garrity (1999) gave periodic expansions for a special cubic family. Murru (arXiv 2013) claimed a periodic representation for every cubic irrational, but the construction depends on the minimal polynomial, and the author's later version says the problem cannot be called completely solved; I could not open that later version. Dasaratha et al. (2012/2014) gave periodic expansions for a broad class of cubic irrationals under a family of algorithms. Jacobs (2019) gave an iff for cubic inputs in a family form and said it does not resolve the problem. Karpenkov (arXiv January 2021; Acta Arithmetica 2022, journal-accepted) proved periodicity of the sin^2-algorithm for totally real cubic irrationals, with the complex-conjugate case stated as open; the Monatshefte article DOI carries 2024 but I could not open it, and whether it is the same argument as the 2021 preprint is unresolved. In-window (after 26 January 2024) the events are: the Monatshefte article (date unverified); Accossato-Murru-Romeo (2025, transcendence, not about the problem as far as the abstract shows; its supposed statement that the problem is open is unverified); the Barclay 2025 'complete characterization' claim (not verifiable: no arXiv identifier, the page returned 403); and two single-author preprints by Ludovic Tagnon (Zenodo 6 July 2026; arXiv 24 and 25 August 2026) addressing the complex-signature cubic case. Tagnon's Part I gives certified periodicity on 205 sample complex cubic polynomials, 194 polynomials in a box, and a Lean-checked plastic-field closure, and says it does not solve the complex case; Part II proves structural identities and gives per-field periodicity only conditional on an unproved hypothesis (C_kappa). Both papers say they were AI-assisted: Part I's Section 9 reads 'This research was AI-assisted.' and 'the human author directed the work and takes responsibility for all claims.'; the Zenodo dataset says 'This work was assisted by AI.'; Part II's Section 9 (as extracted) says 'Parts of the exploratory computations and of the manuscript preparation were AI-assisted'. No model is named in either, so I record no system, but the AI involvement is not nothing: whether the exploratory computations supplied load-bearing mathematics cannot be read from the sentences. No human reviewer, journal, or citing paper engages with the 2026 preprints in the sources I could reach; the Zenodo dataset says no independent mathematician has reviewed the work. Degrees 4 and above show no result in my searches. Close calls: (a) whether Tagnon's sampled certified periodicity counts toward the complex-signature case; (b) whether Murru 2013 counts as a solution of the n=3 instance, given its later caveat; (c) whether Karpenkov's totally real result counts, since its input is a vector of conjugates rather than a single real and its converse is not stated in the abstract I read; (d) the date of the Monatshefte article, which decides whether the 2024 DOI is an in-window event.
competing_reading: Read the 2026 Tagnon papers as real progress on the complex-signature half of the n=3 instance: a deterministic algorithm with exact certificates on every tested field, a Lean-checked plastic closure, and a finite-state structure theory, so that the cubic case has moved in the window even though the general theorem is not proved. Read Karpenkov's Monatshefte article (2024 DOI) and the 2013 Murru claim as settling the n=3 instance (the Monatshefte iff claim for totally real cubic vectors; Murru's 'has been solved'), so the cubic case was settled before the window and the window itself contains no movement except the unverified Barclay claim.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The full text of Karpenkov's Monatshefte article: its publication date, its relation to arXiv 2101.12627, and whether it proves an iff or only forward periodicity. (2) The published International Journal of Number Theory version of Murru (2015) and the Politecnico PDF, to see whether the 'solved' wording survived and what the caveat says. (3) Barclay's arXiv identifier, or confirmation that no such preprint exists. (4) A referee report, journal submission, or expert write-up of Tagnon's Parts I and II, and Paper III. (5) The Lean sources in the Zenodo archive (lean/): whether any sorry remains, and what the sealed theorems state against Problem 4. (6) The Tagnon PDFs read as text, to confirm the verbatim AI sentences and which statements 'proves neither statement' refers to. (7) For the totally real case, whether the sin^2-algorithm's periodic-implies-cubic direction is established and whether it applies to single real inputs. (8) Any result at all for degree 4 or above.

judgement.why: The statement asks, for each n, for one assignment of a natural-number sequence to every real x, with an eventually periodic sequence exactly when x is algebraic of degree n. Each n is an instance, so the classical n=1 and n=2 results are cases, both from long before the snapshot. Everything for n=3 departs from the statement's form. The inputs are conjugate vectors or minimal-polynomial data (Murru, Karpenkov), there is a family of algorithms (Dasaratha, Jacobs), or the setting is p-adic or about transcendence. Those are variants, not cases, and that was the closest call: Karpenkov's totally real result could be read as a case, but it needs a vector of conjugates rather than a single real x, and the record never shows the converse for single real inputs. The Monatshefte DOI has only a year, 2024, so its date cannot be placed. Tagnon Part I says it proves no general theorem and certifies finitely many polynomials and fields, so it is instances. Part II is conditional on an unproved hypothesis (C_kappa), which is a reduction, so none. Both Tagnon papers disclose unnamed AI assistance for 'exploratory computations and manuscript preparation'. No system is recorded and no AI-produced mathematics is identified, so the AI role is none. Barclay's claim has no locatable text and is contradicted by later work, so it is not credible.
judgement.doubts: The Tagnon AI disclosures are vague ('This research was AI-assisted'). If the full text showed that a model produced load-bearing arguments, the AI role could change, but neither event would survive §3 step 1 in any case. Whether Karpenkov's totally real result should count as a case of n=3 depends on reading 'to each real number' as excluding conjugate-vector inputs.
